 Follow Pete Buttigieg splits with Democrats on student loans: No "magic" fix
 Suzanne Blake Mon, November 16, 2026 at 6:46 PM UTC 6 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg has distanced himself from his party's common push for broad student loan forgiveness, saying that Democrats have pushed the issue too far.
 Speaking on Pod Save America on Sunday, Buttigieg said Democrats had "overtorqued" their approach to student loans and questioned the fairness of asking Americans who did not attend college to help shoulder the cost of relief for those who did.
 "I have a very hard time explaining to my relatives in Michigan who did not go to college why they should be paying for people who do," Buttigieg said. "I believe there are ways to make sure that you come out of college debt-free. I believe college should be more affordable. I don't believe in like a magic wand to fix that for everybody who borrowed money."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The new comments put Buttigieg, a former Democratic presidential candidate, at odds with the more aggressive debt-cancellation approach championed by some of his party's leading progressives. Experts told Newsweek their opinions on whether canceling student loans in full is reasonable and fair.
 Why It Matters
 Student loan policy could become a significant point of debate for Democrats as they prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January following their 2026 midterm victories.
 The federal student loan system currently includes 42.3 million borrowers owing more than $1.7 trillion, according to the latest Federal Student Aid data from June. More than 9.3 million of those federal loan recipients were in default.
 Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg speaks during a campaign event for Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DFL) Party candidates at the Northern Midwest Regional Council of Carpenters on November 1, 2026, in St. Paul, Minnesota.
 What Has Pete Buttigieg Said About Student Loan Forgiveness?
 Buttigieg made clear that his disagreement is not with making college more affordable, but with the idea of retroactively eliminating debt for essentially everyone who borrowed.
 Advertisement Advertisement "In the 2020 campaign, I definitely staked out some positions that I still believe in that weren't always kind of popular in the party," Buttigieg said during the Pod Save America interview.
 "One thing is, I think … we really overtorqued on the student loan thing," he said. "As a party, I have a very hard time explaining to my relatives in Michigan who did not go to college why they should be paying for people who do."
 Buttigieg instead emphasized preventing students from accumulating large debts in the first place.
 "I believe there are ways to make sure that you come out of college debt-free," he said. "I believe college should be more affordable. I don't believe in like a magic wand to fix that for everybody who borrowed money."
 Advertisement Advertisement Buttigieg previously served in the administration of former President Joe Biden, and under Biden, the Education Department pursued expansive student debt relief.
 The Supreme Court struck down Biden's original plan for up to $10,000 or $20,000 in cancellation for eligible borrowers in 2023, but his administration continued pursuing targeted relief through existing federal programs.
 "Student loan forgiveness has always raised a legitimate fairness question. How do you explain canceling someone's college debt to a plumber who skipped college. Or a family that sacrificed for years to pay theirs off?" Michael Ryan, a finance expert and the founder of MichaelRyanMoney.com, told Newsweek .
 "But there's another side. Some borrowers have made payments for years, accumulated enormous interest, and barely touched their original balance. That's a problem worth fixing."
 Democrats' Positions on Student Loans and Student Loan Forgiveness
 Buttigieg's criticism comes as Democrats reconsider their student loan agenda following their midterm victories.
 Advertisement Advertisement Democrats do not currently have a single party-wide proposal to cancel student debt across the board, but one approach has focused on eliminating or sharply reducing interest.
 Democratic Representative Joe Courtney of Connecticut and Senator Peter Welch of Vermont introduced the Student Loan Interest Elimination Act in March, a proposal aimed at removing interest from federal student loans rather than canceling borrowers' principal balances.
 "Some lawmakers have proposed potentially capping interest rates on student debt, an idea that may find support from this administration which has signaled willingness in the past to put limits on interest rates to help Americans struggling financially," Alex Beene, a financial literacy instructor for the University of Tennessee at Martin, told Newsweek .
 Democrats have also sought larger Pell Grants and changes to federal borrowing restrictions that were enacted under Republican control.
 Advertisement Advertisement More than 30 Democratic lawmakers also recently pressed Education Secretary Linda McMahon over problems borrowers have reported with their repayment plan transitions and general applications and payment calculations.
 "The larger policy challenge is finding ways to help borrowers genuinely struggling with debt while making college more affordable so future generations don't face the same financial problems," Beene said.
 Moving ahead into the new Congress term next year, some Democrats want significant federal intervention to reduce borrowers' existing financial burdens, while Buttigieg is more focused on making college affordable before students take on debt at all.
 "I don't think his comments will go over well with the large number of young people who decidedly voted blue during the midterms. I feel he is oversimplifying the massive amount of corruption that went on within the higher education system, as so many kids were essentially scammed out of an education," Kevin Thompson, the CEO of 9i Capital Group, told Newsweek .
 Advertisement Advertisement "Much of the Biden era student loan forgiveness was designed to provide relief to disenfranchised borrowers, particularly those who were misled by their institutions. So many kids were left with a worthless diploma, massive student loan balances, or debt from attending schools that are now defunct."
 How Many People Have Student Loan Debt?
 As of June 30, 42.3 million recipients held more than $1.7 trillion in outstanding federal student loans, according to Federal Student Aid. The federal government directly managed 40.5 million borrower accounts totaling more than $1.64 trillion.
 Direct Loans accounted for nearly 91 percent of the outstanding federal loan portfolio, while Federal Family Education Loan Program debt accounted for approximately 9 percent and Perkins loans made up a fraction of 1 percent.
 What Happens Next
 The sheer numbers of those struggling with student loan debt may reflect that something about the system is failing American college students, but outright debt forgiveness may not be the clear answer moving forward, Ryan said.
 Advertisement Advertisement "In my financial planner mind, I'd rather see us fix the loan system that's creating these problems in the first place," Ryan said. "Otherwise, we forgive yesterday's debt while tomorrow's students sign up for the same mess. And I wish politicians could disagree about the details without everyone treating it like a family divorce."
